entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: The standard phrase the person leading a meeting or class uses to open it and move from small talk to the agenda.
entries.usage: Said once most people have arrived, usually after *OK* or *All right*, and often followed by the first topic: *Let's get started with the budget*. It is friendly and neutral, so it fits any meeting, class or workshop. *Let's begin* sounds more formal, and *Let's dive in* or *Let's kick things off* more casual.
entries.pattern: OK / All right, let's get started (with + first topic)
examples: It's a few minutes after ten and almost everyone's here, so **let's get started** with the safety update.
All right, everyone, phones away. **Let's get started** on chapter six.
OK, **let's get started**. The first thing on our list tonight is the spring fundraiser.

drill.sentence: Thanks for coming out on such a rainy night, everyone. It's seven o'clock, so {{let's get started}}.
drill.hint: the standard opener once everyone is here (not *… begin*, *… start* or *… get going*)

entries.related: *let's begin* — more formal; *let's kick things off* — casual, energetic; *let's dive in* — casual, suggests going straight into the details.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: A friendly opening line that thanks people for coming to a call, video meeting or online event.
entries.usage: Standard at the start of video calls, webinars and conference calls, often right before *let's get started*. *Joining* is the typical verb for calls and online events; for people who came into a room, *thanks for coming* is more usual. It also works at the end: *Thanks again for joining, everyone*.
entries.pattern: thanks (everyone) for joining (us / today)
examples: Hi, **thanks everyone for joining** on such short notice. I'll keep this to twenty minutes.
**Thanks for joining**, Dr. Kim. Can you hear us all right on your end?
Good evening, and **thanks for joining** us for tonight's online open house on the library renovation.

drill.sentence: Hi, everyone, {{thanks for joining}}. I know it's early on the West Coast, so I'll keep this short.
drill.hint: the usual short thank-you at the start of a call (not *thank you …* or *… for coming*)

entries.related: *thanks for coming* — for an in-person meeting; *thanks for making the time* — a little warmer, stresses that people are busy; *welcome, everyone* — a host's greeting.

entries.term: the next item on the agenda
entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: The following topic on the written list of topics for a meeting.
entries.usage: Used by the chair to move the meeting forward: *The next item on the agenda is the parking policy*. It is neutral to formal and typical of board, committee and staff meetings with a written agenda. In relaxed meetings, people often just say *Next up…* or *Moving on to…*.
entries.pattern: the next item on the agenda is + topic
examples: **The next item on the agenda** is the new parking policy, so let's hear from Facilities.
Before we move to **the next item on the agenda**, are there any questions about the hiring plan?
After a long debate on the budget, the school board moved on to **the next item on the agenda**: later start times for high schools.

drill.sentence: OK, that's settled. {{The next item on the agenda}} is the date for the holiday party.
drill.hint: the chair's phrase for the following topic on today's written list — six words (the first noun is not *thing*, *topic* or *point*)

entries.related: *agenda item* — any topic on the list; *moving on (to)* — a relaxed way to change topics; *any other business* — British name for the last, open item of an agenda.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces the next topic, speaker or event in a sequence: *Next up is Maria* means that Maria speaks next.
entries.usage: Very common in meetings, classes, conferences, broadcasts and sports commentary, where it sounds lively and informal. It usually starts the sentence and is followed by *is* or *we have*: *Next up, we have the sales numbers*. In a formal board meeting, *The next item is…* is safer.
entries.pattern: Next up is + person / topic; Next up, we have + …
examples: Thanks, Sam, that was really helpful. **Next up** is Maria with the survey results.
**Next up** on tonight's show: a chef who cooks only with vegetables from her own backyard.
**Next up** for the Celtics is a long road trip, starting with Denver on Friday.

drill.sentence: Great job, everyone. {{Next up}}, we have Jamal, who's going to walk us through the new scheduling app.
drill.hint: informal two-word intro for the following speaker (not the reversed form that starts with *Up*)

entries.related: *up next* — same meaning, common on TV and radio; *moving on* — changes the topic; *the next item* — more formal, for meetings with a written agenda.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: A polite way to join a discussion and add a point, often right after someone has finished speaking.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, seminars and calls; *just* makes the request sound small and less like an interruption. It works best in a short pause, but with *Sorry* in front it can also interrupt politely. *If I could just add something* is slightly more formal, and *Can I jump in?* is more casual.
entries.pattern: Can I just add something (here / to that)?
examples: **Can I just add something?** The freezer is already full, so we'll need space before the new samples arrive.
Sorry, **can I just add something** to what Dr. Ruiz said about discharge times?
Before you vote, **can I just add something**? The parking lot also floods every spring.

drill.sentence: Before we move on, {{can I just add something}}? The venue also needs a final head count by Monday.
drill.hint: polite request to make one more point (not *say* or *mention*)

entries.related: *can I jump in?* — casual, often to interrupt; *to build on that* — adds to the last speaker's point; *one more thing* — adds a point to your own turn.

entries.term: I'd like to raise a point
entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: A polite, slightly formal way to bring up an issue so that the group will discuss it.
entries.usage: Common in committee, faculty, board and staff meetings, often with the topic added: *I'd like to raise a point about the schedule*. You can also raise *a concern*, *an issue* or *a question*. In a casual team meeting, *I want to bring something up* sounds more natural.
entries.pattern: I'd like to raise a point (about + topic)
examples: **I'd like to raise a point** that hasn't come up yet: who will cover the night shift in December?
Madam Chair, before we vote, **I'd like to raise a point** about the cost of maintaining the new playground.
Can I go back to the bus routes? **I'd like to raise a point** from the parents' survey.

drill.sentence: Before we close the meeting, {{I'd like to raise a point}} about the noise from the construction site next door.
drill.hint: formally put a matter in front of the group (not *make …*, *bring up …*, *… a concern* or *… an issue*)

entries.related: *make a point* — state an argument, not ask for discussion; *bring something up* — more everyday; *raise a concern* — bring up a possible problem.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To change the time or date of a planned meeting or appointment to a different one.
entries.usage: Very common in emails and calls, usually with a short reason and an apology: *Could we reschedule for Thursday?* The new time follows *for* or *to*. *Reschedule* can move a meeting earlier or later, while *postpone* only moves it later; Americans pronounce it *re-SKED-jool*.
entries.pattern: reschedule (a meeting) for / to + new time
examples: Something came up at my daughter's school, so could we **reschedule** our meeting for Thursday?
The surgeon had an emergency, and the clinic **rescheduled** my appointment twice in one week.
The board had to **reschedule the meeting** because too few members could attend.

drill.sentence: I'm stuck at the airport, so we'll need to {{reschedule}} tomorrow's meeting for next week.
drill.hint: change it to a different time (not *postpone* or *move*)

entries.related: *postpone* — move to a later time; *push back* — informal, move later; *move up* (US) — move earlier; *cancel* — stop it from happening at all.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An electronic meeting invitation, sent through a calendar app such as Outlook or Google Calendar, that adds the event to the receiver's calendar.
entries.usage: Standard in office talk and email, as in *I'll send you a calendar invite*, often shortened to *an invite*. The noun *invite* is informal but normal at work, and it is stressed on the first syllable, *IN-vite*. You *accept* or *decline* an invite; in formal writing, say *invitation*.
entries.pattern: send (someone) a calendar invite (for + event)
examples: Thursday at two works for me. I'll send you **a calendar invite** with the Zoom link.
I accepted **the calendar invite**, but it showed up in the wrong time zone on my phone.
My sister sent the whole family **a calendar invite** for Mom's surprise party.

drill.sentence: Once we agree on a time, Priya will send everyone {{a calendar invite}} so nobody books something else in that slot.
drill.hint: electronic meeting request that adds the event to their app — three words (not *a meeting …*)

entries.related: *a meeting request* — Outlook's formal name for it; *a save-the-date* — an early notice for a big event; *an invitation* — the formal noun.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Meetings scheduled directly one after another, with no break in between.
entries.usage: Common in work talk, usually to explain why you are slow to reply or late: *Sorry, I've been in back-to-back meetings all day*. It often sounds like a mild complaint about a busy schedule. The phrase works for other events too: *back-to-back flights*, *back-to-back games*.
entries.pattern: be in back-to-back meetings (all day / all morning)
examples: Sorry for the slow reply; I've been in **back-to-back meetings** since eight this morning.
On Mondays the head nurse has **back-to-back meetings**, so try to catch her before nine.
Don't schedule **back-to-back meetings** all afternoon; you'll need time to eat and think.

drill.sentence: I can't call you until five; I have {{back-to-back meetings}} all afternoon.
drill.hint: one session right after another, hyphenated (not *nonstop* or *wall-to-wall*)

entries.related: *wall-to-wall meetings* — informal, the whole day is full; *a packed schedule* — a very full day; *a buffer* — a short free gap you leave between meetings.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A short report on where a task or project stands now: what is done, what is next and any problems.
entries.usage: Common in project teams, emails and short daily meetings: *Can you give us a quick status update on the move?* It is neutral and businesslike, and managers often ask for one in writing. In casual talk, people say *Where are we on…?* or *Any news on…?*
entries.pattern: give / send / get a (quick) status update (on something)
examples: Could each group leader give **a status update** before we discuss the new deadline?
Our contractor sends **a status update** every Friday with photos of the kitchen.
The airline sent **a status update** every half hour, but none of them said when we'd actually take off.

drill.sentence: My manager asked for {{a status update}} on the website redesign: what's finished and what's still left.
drill.hint: a short report on current progress (not *a progress report*)

entries.related: *a progress report* — longer and more formal, often written; *a check-in* — a short conversation that may include an update; *an update* — the general word.

entries.term: does anyone have anything to add?
entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: A question the chair asks to invite more comments before the group moves on or ends the meeting.
entries.usage: Typically asked at the end of an agenda item or of the whole meeting, followed by a short pause so people can speak. It is neutral and polite. *Anything else?* is the casual version, and with one person you can say *Ben, anything to add?*
examples: That's my update on the renovation. **Does anyone have anything to add?**
Before we close the case review, **does anyone have anything to add** about the patient's discharge?
The coach looked around the locker room and asked, "**Does anyone have anything to add?**"

drill.sentence: OK, I think we've covered the schedule. {{Does anyone have anything to add}} before we move on?
drill.hint: invites any further comments from the group (not *Any questions*)

entries.related: *any other comments?* — slightly more formal; *anything else?* — short and casual; *any questions?* — asks only for questions, not new points.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To ask for and receive someone's ideas, opinion or advice on a plan or piece of work.
entries.usage: A neutral, collaborative phrase common in meetings and emails: *I'd like to get your input on the schedule*. It signals that the other person's view matters, so it is a polite way to involve a senior colleague or a client. *Input* in this sense is normally uncountable: *your input*, not *your inputs*.
entries.pattern: get someone's input on something; I'd love your input
examples: Before we order the new microscope, I'd like to **get your input** on which model to choose.
The city is holding a public meeting to **get residents' input** on the new bike lanes.
We wanted to **get the kids' input** before booking our summer vacation.

drill.sentence: Your team uses the system every day, so I'd like to {{get your input}} on the new design before we finalize it.
drill.hint: obtain the view of the people who use it — *get* + possessive + noun (not *feedback*, *thoughts* or *opinion*)

mistake.wrong: Thanks for all your inputs on the draft.
mistake.right: Thanks for all your input on the draft.
mistake.why: In American English, *input* meaning ideas or opinions is normally uncountable, so it has no plural.

entries.related: *feedback* — comments on something already done; *thoughts* — casual, *any thoughts?*; *buy-in* — agreement and support, not just ideas.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To produce many ideas quickly, often in a group, without judging or rejecting any of them yet.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, classrooms and creative work: *Let's brainstorm some names for the app*. It takes a direct object (*brainstorm ideas, names, solutions*) or none, and the activity is called *brainstorming* or *a brainstorming session*. The point is many ideas first and judging later, so it sounds open and collaborative.
entries.pattern: brainstorm (ideas / names / solutions) (for something)
examples: Let's spend ten minutes **brainstorming** ways to cut our cloud costs before we judge any of them.
The fourth-graders **brainstormed** names for the class hamster and then voted.
Over dinner, my partner and I **brainstormed ideas** for a cheap anniversary trip.

drill.sentence: Grab a sticky note, everyone. We're going to {{brainstorm}} as many ideas as we can for the fundraiser, and nothing is too silly.
drill.hint: suggest freely and quickly, judging later — one verb (not *come up with* or *generate*)

entries.related: *come up with* — think of an idea, alone or in a group; *bounce ideas off someone* — test your ideas by talking to someone; *a whiteboard session* — informal, a meeting to sketch ideas.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To let the other people on a video call see what is on your computer screen.
entries.usage: Standard on Zoom, Teams and similar calls: *Can you share your screen?* or *Let me share my screen*. You *stop sharing* when you are done, and people often check with *Can everyone see my screen?* It is neutral and fine with anyone, from a colleague to a client.
entries.pattern: share your / my screen; stop sharing
examples: Let me **share my screen** so you can all see the latest version of the floor plan.
Could you **share your screen**? I can't find the file you're talking about.
My grandmother learned to **share her screen** so she could show us her vacation photos on Zoom.

drill.sentence: We can hear you, Dana, but we can't see the slides. Could you {{share your screen}} again?
drill.hint: let everyone on the call view your display (not *show us*)

entries.related: *screen-share* — informal verb and noun; *present* — the button name in some apps; *stop sharing* — end it.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To agree on a date and time that works for everyone who needs to be at a meeting or event.
entries.usage: Very common in emails and at the end of calls: *Let's find a time to talk next week*. It sounds cooperative because the scheduling is shared. In emails it is often followed by an offer, such as a few free slots or a link to a scheduling tool.
entries.pattern: find a time (to meet / talk) that works (for everyone)
examples: I'd love to hear more about your project. Can we **find a time to meet** next week?
With five kids' schedules, it's hard to **find a time** when the whole family can eat together.
The committee struggled to **find a time** that worked for members in three time zones.

drill.sentence: I'm traveling until Wednesday, but let's {{find a time}} later in the week to go over your résumé.
drill.hint: agree on a slot that suits us both — three words (not *pick …*, *set up …* or *schedule*)

entries.related: *set up a meeting* — arrange it; *what works for you?* — asks for someone's free times; *a scheduling poll* — a tool that lets a group vote on times.

entries.term: could you say more about that?
entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: A polite, natural request for someone to explain their point in more detail.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, interviews, seminars and doctor's visits. It sounds interested rather than critical, so it is softer than *What do you mean?* A more casual version is *Tell me more*, and *Could you elaborate?* is more formal.
examples: You mentioned that the new protocol causes delays. **Could you say more about that?**
**Could you say more about** why the second option is riskier? I'm not sure I follow.
When I told my doctor I'd been sleeping badly, she asked, "**Could you say more about that?**"

drill.sentence: You said the trip was "complicated." {{Could you say more about that}}?
drill.hint: politely asking for further detail (not *tell me* or *elaborate*)

entries.related: *could you elaborate (on that)?* — more formal; *what do you mean?* — can sound challenging; *could you give an example?* — asks for something concrete.

entries.term: we have a lot to cover
entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: An opening line that tells the group there are many topics to discuss, so the meeting needs to move quickly.
entries.usage: Said at the start of a meeting, class or training, usually as a polite signal to skip small talk and stay focused: *We have a lot to cover today, so let's dive in*. It is neutral and fits any setting. *We've got a lot to get through* means the same and is a little more casual.
entries.pattern: We have a lot to cover (today), so …
examples: **We have a lot to cover** today, so let's keep each update to two minutes.
Grab your coffee and sit down, everyone; **we have a lot to cover** before Friday's health inspection.
The tour guide warned us that **we had a lot to cover**, so there'd be no time for shopping.

drill.sentence: Let's skip the introductions; {{we have a lot to cover}} and only forty-five minutes.
drill.hint: there are many topics today — six words, no *got* (not *… get through* or *… discuss*)

entries.related: *we've got a lot to get through* — more casual; *we have a full agenda* — slightly more formal; *in the interest of time* — explains why you are cutting something short.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To come back to a topic, plan or decision later in order to discuss it or think about it again.
entries.usage: Common in meetings and emails, often to postpone a decision politely: *Let's revisit this in the spring*. It sounds open and reasonable, and it can suggest that an earlier decision might change. It is more formal than *come back to* and less jargon-like than *circle back*.
entries.pattern: revisit + topic / decision (in + time / once …)
examples: We don't have the cost estimates yet, so let's **revisit** the question next month.
After a year of rising rent, we **revisited** the idea of buying a house.
The school district plans to **revisit** its cellphone ban at the end of the school year.

drill.sentence: The board rejected the proposal in 2023, but it agreed to {{revisit}} it once the new budget is approved.
drill.hint: come back to it and discuss it again — one verb (not *reconsider* or *review*)

entries.related: *come back to* — plainer, everyday; *circle back (to)* — American office jargon; *reconsider* — think again about a decision, with a real chance of changing it.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To write the official notes of a meeting, recording who attended, what was discussed and what was decided.
entries.usage: Used for formal or regular meetings such as boards, committees and faculty meetings. *Minutes* is plural here (*the minutes were approved*): you *take* them during the meeting, *circulate* them afterward and *approve* them at the next meeting. In informal teams, people just say *take notes*.
entries.pattern: take (the) minutes; approve the minutes
examples: Could someone **take the minutes** today? Our usual secretary is out sick.
As the newest member of the PTA, I was asked to **take minutes** at every meeting.
The department secretary **takes the minutes**, and they're posted online about a week later.

drill.sentence: Since you're not presenting today, could you {{take the minutes}} and send them around afterward?
drill.hint: write the official record of the meeting (not *… notes*)

entries.related: *take notes* — informal, for your own use or a small team; *meeting notes* — a less formal written summary; *the record* — a formal word for what was officially said.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To lead a meeting: open and close it, follow the agenda and decide who speaks.
entries.usage: Used for formal meetings, committees, panels and conference sessions, and the person is called *the chair*. It is neutral and appears in both speech and writing. For informal team meetings, people more often say *run* or *lead the meeting*.
entries.pattern: chair a meeting / committee / session / panel
examples: Dr. Okoye will **chair** the meeting while the department head is on leave.
She **chaired** the hiring committee and kept every discussion fair and on time.
I've never **chaired a meeting** before, so I wrote out exactly what to say at the start.

drill.sentence: You've been on the committee the longest, so would you be willing to {{chair}} it next year?
drill.hint: be its formal leader — one verb (not *run*, *lead* or *head*)

entries.related: *run a meeting* — everyday; *facilitate* — guide a discussion without controlling the decision; *moderate* — lead a panel or debate.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To send a document to all the people in a group, for example before or after a meeting.
entries.usage: Common in work emails and meetings: *I'll circulate the agenda by Friday*. It is a bit formal and sounds organized; in casual speech, people say *send around* or *send out*. It is often passive: *The draft was circulated to all members*.
entries.pattern: circulate something (to + group) (before / after + event)
examples: I'll **circulate** the agenda on Monday so everyone has time to read the reports.
The draft policy was **circulated** to all staff for comments before the vote.
Someone **circulated** a petition in our building to get the elevator fixed.

drill.sentence: Please read the draft budget that Karen {{circulated}} last week before you come to Thursday's meeting.
drill.hint: sent to the whole group — formal verb (not *shared*, *distributed* or *sent out*)

entries.related: *send around* — everyday; *distribute* — formal, often for printed copies; *share* — common for online documents.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To start talking about or doing something else and lose focus on the main topic or task.
entries.usage: Common in meetings and daily life, often as a gentle admission: *Sorry, I got sidetracked*. It describes something that happens by accident, not on purpose. A chair can say *Let's not get sidetracked* to pull a discussion back to the topic.
entries.pattern: get sidetracked (by something)
examples: We **got sidetracked** arguing about the office coffee machine and never discussed the budget.
I meant to clean the garage, but I **got sidetracked** looking through old photos.
Let's not **get sidetracked**; the only question today is whether we hire one nurse or two.

drill.sentence: Sorry, I {{got sidetracked}}. What I was trying to say is that the bus leaves at seven, not eight.
drill.hint: drifted away from my main point — *got* + one word (not *distracted*)

entries.related: *go off on a tangent* — start talking about an unrelated topic; *get off track* — lose focus; *get back on track* — return to the main topic.

entries.spoken_term: let's turn to the next item
entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: A phrase for moving the discussion to a new topic: *Let's turn to the budget* means let's start discussing the budget now.
entries.usage: Neutral and a little formal, common for chairs, teachers, panel moderators and news anchors. It is followed by the topic: *Let's turn to the budget*, *Let's turn now to question three*. In a casual team meeting, *Let's move on to…* is more common.
entries.pattern: let's turn (now) to + topic
examples: Thanks, Leo. **Let's turn to** the hiring plan, which is the main item for today.
We have about ten minutes left, so **let's turn to** your questions.
On the evening news, the anchor said, "Now **let's turn to** sports," and the highlights began.

drill.sentence: That settles the date. Now {{let's turn to}} the menu, which is where we really need your help.
drill.hint: we'll now start discussing — three words, chair style (not *move on to*, *move to*, *talk about* or *look at*)

entries.related: *let's move on to* — more casual; *moving on* — even shorter; *that brings us to* — links one topic to the next.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A quick question asking about the current status or progress of a task or project.
entries.usage: Very common in American workplaces, in meetings, chat and email: *Where are we on the contract?* It is direct and efficient, but from a manager it can feel like gentle pressure if the task is late. *Where are we with…?* is also common, and *Any update on…?* is a softer written version.
entries.pattern: Where are we on + task / project?
examples: **Where are we on** the grant report? It's due to the foundation on Friday.
Hey, **where are we on** the vacation plans? Flights are getting more expensive every day.
The head chef leaned over the counter and called, "**Where are we on** table six?"

drill.sentence: Hi Tom, quick question: {{where are we on}} the new website? The client asked me about it this morning.
drill.hint: asking for the current status — informal US, four words (not *… with*)

entries.related: *any update on…?* — softer, common in writing; *how's … coming along?* — friendly; *what's the status of…?* — neutral, a little more formal.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: There is very little time left in the meeting or activity, so the group must finish or speed up.
entries.usage: Said by the chair or a speaker as a polite signal to wrap up: *We're running out of time, so let's take one last question*. It is neutral and common in meetings, classes and talks. *We're almost out of time* means the same; *We're out of time* means there is none left.
entries.pattern: We're running out of time, so …
examples: **We're running out of time**, so let's take just one more question from the audience.
Hurry up and pick a dessert; **we're running out of time** before the movie starts.
Down by one goal with two minutes left, the team knew **they were running out of time**.

drill.sentence: {{We're running out of time}}, so I'll skip the last two slides and go straight to the summary.
drill.hint: only a few minutes remain — progressive form (not *almost out of …*)

entries.related: *we're almost out of time* — same meaning; *we're at time* — US, the end has come; *we're short on time* — there isn't much time, often from the start.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: Invites a particular person or group to speak next, often to report or to give their view.
entries.usage: Used by a chair, host or teacher to pass the turn to someone: *Let's hear from Maya on the survey results*. It is warm and neutral and suits meetings, panels and classes. It can also invite quieter people in: *Let's hear from someone who hasn't spoken yet*.
entries.pattern: Let's hear from + person / group (on + topic)
examples: Thanks for the overview. Now **let's hear from** the night nurses, who see this problem every shift.
OK, **let's hear from** the other side of the room. What do you all think?
On the radio show, the host said, "**Let's hear from** a listener who's calling in from Ohio."

drill.sentence: Engineering has had its say. Now {{let's hear from}} Marketing, since they'll be selling the product.
drill.hint: invite them to speak next (not *turn to*, *go to* or *ask*)

entries.related: *over to you* — hands the turn to one person; *the floor is yours* — more ceremonial; *let's go around the room* — everyone speaks in turn.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: Tells someone that it is now their turn to speak to the group.
entries.usage: Used by a chair, host or moderator to hand over to a speaker, especially in talks, panels and formal meetings; *the floor* here means the right to speak. It is polite and a little ceremonial, so in a casual team meeting it can sound slightly playful. *Go ahead* and *Take it away* are more casual.
examples: Our next speaker runs the sleep clinic at the university hospital. Dr. Chen, **the floor is yours**.
When the council president said, "**The floor is yours**," the first resident stepped up to the microphone.
Our teacher sat down at the back of the room and said, "OK, Group 3, **the floor is yours**."

drill.sentence: OK, that's it for the budget. Ben, {{the floor is yours}}: tell us about the new training plan.
drill.hint: it's your turn to address the group (not *over to you*, *go ahead*, *take it away* or *it's all …*)

entries.related: *have the floor* — be the one allowed to speak; *give someone the floor* — let them speak; *open the floor (to questions)* — let the audience speak.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: A formal way to suggest a plan or decision for the group to discuss and decide on.
entries.usage: Common in committee, board and faculty meetings and in formal emails. In American English, the verb after *propose that* is usually in the base form: *I'd like to propose that she lead the project* / *that the meeting be moved*. In a casual team meeting, *What if we…?* or *How about we…?* sounds more relaxed.
entries.pattern: I'd like to propose that + subject + base verb
examples: **I'd like to propose that** we postpone the vote until everyone has read the report.
**I'd like to propose that** the clinic open an hour earlier on Saturdays.
At the condo meeting, my dad stood up and said, "**I'd like to propose that** we hire a new landscaper."

drill.sentence: Since half the team works remotely, {{I'd like to propose that}} all staff meetings be held online.
drill.hint: formally put forward the plan — five words, polite form (not *suggest*, *recommend* or *move*)

entries.related: *I suggest (that) we…* — a little less formal; *I move that…* — very formal, used to make an official motion; *What if we…?* — casual.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the group that all the planned topics have been discussed, usually as a signal that the meeting can end.
entries.usage: Said by the chair near the end, usually followed by thanks or a last check for questions. *I think* softens it and leaves room for others to add something. When only your own part is finished, say *That's it from me*.
examples: OK, **I think that covers everything**. Thanks, everyone, and see you next Tuesday.
**I think that covers everything** on the packing list, unless you want to bring the tent.
The nurse went through my discharge instructions and said, "**I think that covers everything**."

drill.sentence: We've gone through the budget, the schedule and the new hires, so {{I think that covers everything}}. Thanks for your time.
drill.hint: all the planned topics have been discussed — five words (not *that's it* or *that's all*)

entries.related: *if there's nothing else* — invites last points before closing; *let's wrap up* — let's finish; *that's it from me* — my part is done.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To post a link, file or short note in the text chat of a video call or online meeting.
entries.usage: Very common on Zoom and Teams calls: *I'll drop the link in the chat*. *Drop* makes it sound quick and casual, which is normal in most work calls. *Post* or *put* it in the chat are neutral alternatives.
entries.pattern: drop + link / file / question in the chat
examples: I'll **drop the link in the chat** so you can all download the slides after the call.
If you have questions during the webinar, just **drop them in the chat**, and I'll answer at the end.
During our family video call, my cousin **dropped** a photo of the new puppy **in the chat**.

drill.sentence: We can't hear your question, Mark. Could you {{drop it in the chat}} instead?
drill.hint: write it in the call's text window — casual verb (not *type*, *put*, *post* or *throw*)

entries.related: *put something in the chat* — neutral; *the chat* — the text window of a video call; *a chat thread* — a running conversation in an app like Slack or Teams.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To open a file, web page or record so that it appears on a screen.
entries.usage: Very common in speech at work and in daily life: *Let me pull up the spreadsheet*. It is informal but fine in any meeting. A noun object can go before or after *up* (*pull up the file*, *pull the file up*), but a pronoun must go before it: *pull it up*, not *pull up it*.
entries.pattern: pull up + file / page; pull it up (on + screen)
examples: Hang on, let me **pull up** last quarter's numbers so we're all looking at the same thing.
The pharmacist **pulled up** my prescription history and found the problem right away.
Can you **pull up** a map? I have no idea where this restaurant is.

drill.sentence: I don't remember the exact date, but give me a second and I'll {{pull it up}} on my laptop.
drill.hint: open it so it shows on the screen — phrasal verb (not *look … up* or *bring … up*)

entries.related: *bring up* — also used for showing something on a screen; *look up* — search for a piece of information; *open* — the neutral verb.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To reserve a period in your calendar for one task, so that nobody can book a meeting then.
entries.usage: Common in American offices with shared calendars: *I've blocked off Friday mornings for writing*. It shows that the time is protected, not free. *Block out time* means the same, and the reserved period is often called *a time block* or *focus time*.
entries.pattern: block off (time / an hour / Friday morning) (for + task)
examples: I've **blocked off** two hours every morning for writing, so please don't book meetings then.
Our pediatrician **blocks off time** at the end of each day for kids who need to be seen right away.
We **blocked off** the whole weekend to paint the nursery before the baby arrives.

drill.sentence: My calendar fills up fast, so I {{block off time}} every Friday afternoon to answer emails.
drill.hint: reserve a period in my calendar (not *set aside*, *make* or *… out*)

entries.related: *block out time* — same meaning; *set aside time* — keep time free for something, not only in a calendar; *protect your time* — refuse meetings in reserved periods.

entries.term: the purpose of this meeting is to …
entries.spoken_term: the purpose of this meeting is to
entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: States the main goal of a meeting at the start, so that everyone knows what it should achieve.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, used by the chair right after the greeting: *The purpose of this meeting is to agree on a timeline*. It keeps the discussion focused, and you can point back to it if people drift. In relaxed meetings, *The goal today is to…* sounds less formal.
entries.pattern: The purpose of this meeting is to + verb
examples: **The purpose of this meeting is to** agree on a schedule for the clinic renovation.
Just to be clear, **the purpose of this meeting is to** listen, not to make any decisions yet.
The principal began by saying, "**The purpose of this meeting is to** explain the new pickup rules."

drill.sentence: Good morning, everyone. {{The purpose of this meeting is to}} choose a vendor for the new phone system.
drill.hint: states today's goal (not *The goal …*, *The aim …* or *The point …*)

entries.related: *the goal today is to* — less formal; *what I'd like us to get out of today is* — relaxed and personal; *the agenda* — the list of topics, not the goal.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To add a topic to the list of things that a meeting will discuss.
entries.usage: Common in emails before a meeting: *Could we put the travel budget on the agenda?* It is neutral and polite, and it is a good way to make sure a topic gets discussed instead of raising it at the last minute. *Add something to the agenda* means the same.
entries.pattern: put something on the agenda (for + meeting)
examples: Can we **put** the broken air conditioning **on the agenda** for next week's staff meeting?
If no one **puts** it **on the agenda**, the leaky roof will never get discussed.
I'll **put** your request **on the agenda**, but I can't promise the board will approve it.

drill.sentence: Lunch breaks for the night shift keep coming up. Can we {{put it on the agenda}} for Monday's meeting?
drill.hint: include it in the list of topics to discuss (not *add … to*)

entries.related: *add something to the agenda* — same meaning; *take something off the agenda* — remove it; *high on the agenda* — an important priority, also outside meetings.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To have two appointments or meetings arranged for the same time, usually by mistake.
entries.usage: Common at work and in daily life, usually as part of an apology: *Sorry, I'm double-booked at three*. People also say *I double-booked myself*. A room, a table or a hotel room can be *double-booked* too, when two people have reserved it.
entries.pattern: be double-booked (at + time); double-book yourself
examples: I'm so sorry, I'm **double-booked** at two. Could we move our call to four?
The restaurant had **double-booked** our table, so we waited forty minutes at the bar.
I accidentally **double-booked myself** and promised to be at two birthday parties on Saturday.

drill.sentence: Sorry, I can't make the four o'clock call after all. I'm {{double-booked}}: I also have a dentist appointment then.
drill.hint: have two commitments at the same moment (not *busy* or *tied up*)

entries.related: *have a conflict* — have another commitment at that time, more neutral; *overbooked* — a flight or hotel sold more places than it has; *tied up* — busy.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Refers back to a point that another person has already made, often to agree with it or build on it.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, seminars and writing: *As Sarah pointed out, the timeline is tight*. It gives credit to the other person, which sounds collaborative and polite. Use a name or a group (*as several people pointed out*); in a written text, *as noted above* refers to an earlier part.
entries.pattern: As + person + pointed out (earlier), …
examples: **As Jake pointed out**, we can't start recruiting patients until the review board approves the study.
**As my mother pointed out**, the cheaper apartment is a long way from any grocery store.
**As several readers pointed out**, the article got the date of the flood wrong.

drill.sentence: As Maria {{pointed out}} earlier, the room only holds forty people, so we'll need a bigger space.
drill.hint: drew attention to — phrasal verb (not *said*, *mentioned* or *noted*)

entries.related: *as someone mentioned* — more neutral; *to build on what someone said* — adds to their point; *as someone rightly said* — stronger agreement.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To be present at a meeting, class or event.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in emails, forms and reports: *Over thirty people attended the meeting*. *Attend* takes a direct object with no preposition; *attend to* means deal with or take care of something. In casual speech, people more often say *go to* or *be at* a meeting.
entries.pattern: attend + meeting / class / conference (no preposition)
examples: Unfortunately, I won't be able to **attend the meeting** on Thursday because I'll be traveling.
About two hundred residents **attended** the public meeting about the new highway exit.
My grandfather still **attends** every home game, even in the snow.

drill.sentence: Only five people {{attended}} the condo association meeting, so the vote had to be postponed.
drill.hint: were present at — one verb, no preposition (not *came to* or *went to*)

mistake.wrong: I will attend to the meeting on Monday.
mistake.right: I will attend the meeting on Monday.
mistake.why: *Attend* takes a direct object; *attend to* means deal with or take care of something.

entries.related: *go to* / *be at* — everyday; *sit in on* — attend without taking an active part; *miss* — not attend.

entries.label: verb + adverb
entries.meaning: To take part in a meeting or event by video or phone instead of being there in person.
entries.usage: Very common in meeting invitations and emails since hybrid work spread: *I'll join remotely from home*. It is neutral and fine in any setting. The opposite is *join in person*; *dial in* is also used, especially for phone calls.
entries.pattern: join (the meeting) remotely / in person
examples: I'm home with a sick kid today, so I'll **join remotely** if that's OK.
Students who live more than fifty miles away can **join** the seminar **remotely**.
Grandpa couldn't travel, so he **joined** the wedding **remotely** from his living room.

drill.sentence: Can't make it to the staff meeting in person? You can {{join remotely}}; the link is in the calendar invite.
drill.hint: take part by video instead of in person — verb + adverb (not *… online* or *dial in*)

entries.related: *in person* — physically there; *hybrid meeting* — some people in the room, some online; *dial in* — join by phone or video.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite formula you say just before you leave a meeting, conversation or room.
entries.usage: Used when you have to leave before others, often with a short reason: *If you'll excuse me, I have another call at two*. It is polite and slightly formal. With colleagues you know well, *Sorry, I have to jump off* (on a call) or *I need to head out* is more casual.
entries.pattern: If you'll excuse me, I need to / I have to …
examples: **If you'll excuse me**, I have to step out for another meeting, but Ana will finish the presentation.
**If you'll excuse me**, I need to check on the kids; they've gone very quiet.
The doctor said, "**If you'll excuse me**, I have a patient waiting," and left the room.

drill.sentence: It was lovely talking to you both. Now, {{if you'll excuse me}}, I need to find my wife before the speeches start.
drill.hint: politely asking permission to leave — four words (not *pardon me*)

entries.related: *excuse me* — short, also to get past someone or get attention; *I'll let you go* — politely ends a conversation for the other person's sake; *I need to head out* — casual.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A meeting that achieves useful results, such as clear decisions and next steps.
entries.usage: Very common as a polite comment at the end of a meeting or in a follow-up email: *Thanks, everyone, that was a really productive meeting*. It is neutral to slightly formal and is sometimes said out of politeness even when little was achieved. The opposite is *an unproductive meeting* or, casually, *a waste of time*.
examples: Thanks, everyone, that was **a productive meeting**. We finally have a launch date.
After **a productive meeting** with the landlord, we agreed to split the cost of the repairs.
The parent-teacher conference turned into **a** surprisingly **productive meeting** about my son's reading.

drill.sentence: We made three decisions and gave every task an owner, so I'd call that {{a productive meeting}}.
drill.hint: one that achieved useful results (not *good*, *useful* or *successful*)

entries.related: *a good meeting* — more casual; *a waste of time* — the opposite, informal; *this could have been an email* — a joke about a pointless meeting.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: The scheduled end of the meeting has come, so the group needs to stop now.
entries.usage: Common in American work meetings and calls, said by the chair to close on schedule: *Looks like we're at time, so let's pick this up next week*. It is efficient and polite, since it respects people's next meetings. It is mostly American office language; *We're out of time* means the same and is understood everywhere.
examples: Looks like **we're at time**, so let's pick up the budget discussion on Thursday.
Sorry to cut you off, Dev, but **we're at time**, and some people have a class at noon.
The webinar host said **we were at time** but promised to answer the remaining questions by email.

drill.sentence: It's 10:59, so {{we're at time}}. I'll send the notes, and we'll pick this up next Monday.
drill.hint: the meeting's planned end has arrived — short US office phrase (not *… out of …*)

entries.related: *we're out of time* — same, understood everywhere; *we're running out of time* — little time is left; *run over* — continue past the planned end.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To keep a meeting or activity going at a good pace, so that it does not slow down or get stuck.
entries.usage: Often said by the chair as a polite reason to cut a discussion short: *Just to keep things moving, let's save questions for the end*. It sounds friendly and practical, not rude. It is also used for any process that must not stall, from a kitchen to a court case.
entries.pattern: (just) to keep things moving, …
examples: Just to **keep things moving**, let's hold questions until the end of each presentation.
The wedding planner's job was to **keep things moving** so dinner wasn't served at midnight.
When the case stalled, the judge set strict deadlines to **keep things moving**.

drill.sentence: We have twelve updates to get through, so I'll {{keep things moving}} and stop anyone who goes over two minutes.
drill.hint: maintain a good pace (not *… on track* or *move … along*)

entries.related: *keep us on track* — keep the group on the planned topics; *move things along* — speed things up; *get bogged down* — get stuck in details.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To limit a meeting, talk or activity to a certain length, so that it does not go over.
entries.usage: Common when you set up or start a meeting: *I'll keep it to 30 minutes*. It is a polite promise or request that respects people's time. The object can change (*keep your talk to ten minutes*, *keep the speeches to two minutes each*), and *keep it under an hour* sets a maximum.
entries.pattern: keep it / the meeting / your talk to + length
examples: I know it's a busy week, so I'll **keep it to 30 minutes** and send the details by email.
Each speaker at the wedding was asked to **keep it to** two minutes, but the best man talked for ten.
The kids can play video games on school nights, but we **keep it to** an hour.

drill.sentence: The principal has a busy afternoon, so she asked us to {{keep it to}} fifteen minutes.
drill.hint: make sure the meeting runs no longer than — three words (not *… under*)

entries.related: *keep it short* — be brief; *keep it under (an hour)* — less than that length; *a hard stop* — a fixed time when someone must leave.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Let's keep this meeting or conversation short, because there is little time or little to discuss.
entries.usage: Said at the start of a short call or chat: *I know you're busy, so let's make this quick*. It sounds friendly between colleagues, but from a boss or to a client it can seem impatient. *I'll keep this short* is softer, because it is about you, not the other person.
examples: I have a train to catch, so **let's make this quick**: are we going with the red logo or the blue one?
**Let's make this quick**; the parking meter runs out in ten minutes.
The real estate agent said, "**Let's make this quick**; I have three more showings today."

drill.sentence: I only have ten minutes before my next class, so {{let's make this quick}}.
drill.hint: ask for a brief exchange — informal, four words, object *this* (not *keep … short*)

entries.related: *I'll keep this short* — softer, about your own talk; *I won't keep you long* — polite, promises a short conversation; *in a nutshell* — briefly.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A meeting held after an event, task or project to discuss how it went and what to do better next time.
entries.usage: Common in companies, hospitals, schools and event teams: *Let's do a quick debrief after the launch*. It is also a verb (*debrief the team*); the noun is usually stressed on the first syllable and the verb on the second. Software teams call a review after a failure *a postmortem* and a regular team review *a retro*.
entries.pattern: do / have / hold a (quick) debrief (after + event)
examples: After the conference, the organizers held **a debrief** to list what worked and what didn't.
The ER team does **a quick debrief** after every difficult case.
After the school trip, the teachers met for **a debrief** over pizza.

drill.sentence: The launch is Friday. Let's hold {{a debrief}} on Monday to talk about what went well and what we'd change.
drill.hint: a meeting afterward to look back on how it went (not *a review*, *a wrap-up*, *a retro* or *a postmortem*)

entries.related: *a postmortem* — a review after something failed; *a retrospective* (*retro*) — a regular team review in software; *a wrap-up* — a short closing meeting.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: Asks whether anyone disagrees before the group makes a decision or goes ahead.
entries.usage: Used by a chair right after stating a proposal, followed by a short pause. If nobody speaks, the group is taken to agree, so it is a quick way to decide without a formal vote. The fuller form is *Are there any objections?*
examples: Let's move the team lunch to Thursdays from now on. **Any objections?**
Let's approve last month's minutes as written. **Any objections?** Great, they're approved.
"We're ordering Thai food tonight. **Any objections?**" Dad asked, already holding the phone.

drill.sentence: The proposal is to move the book club to the first Tuesday of the month. {{Any objections}}? Then it's decided.
drill.hint: asks whether anyone disagrees — two words (not *… questions* or *… concerns*)

entries.related: *any concerns?* — softer, invites worries, not only disagreement; *all in favor?* — starts a vote; *do we have consensus?* — asks if everyone agrees.

entries.label: meeting phrase
entries.meaning: A closing phrase meaning that if nobody has more to discuss, the meeting can end.
entries.usage: Said by the chair at the end of a meeting, usually followed by a short pause in case someone does have more. It is polite and neutral. Common continuations are *…let's wrap up*, *…we can end early* and *…thanks, everyone*.
entries.pattern: If there's nothing else, let's wrap up / we'll end here
examples: **If there's nothing else**, let's wrap up and give everyone ten minutes back.
The loan officer closed the folder and said, "**If there's nothing else**, I'll have the papers ready by Friday."
Our book club leader always ends with "**If there's nothing else**, same time next month."

drill.sentence: OK, we've covered the schedule and the budget. {{If there's nothing else}}, we can finish ten minutes early.
drill.hint: if nobody has more to discuss (not *If that's all* or *If that's everything*)

entries.related: *I think that covers everything* — all topics are done; *let's wrap up* — let's finish; *any other business?* — British, asks for last topics.

entries.term: let's give it a couple more minutes
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Let's wait a little longer before starting, so that people who are late can still arrive or join.
entries.usage: Very common at the start of calls and meetings when only a few people are there: *Let's give it a couple more minutes for people to join*. It is relaxed and polite. Note *a couple more minutes*, with no *of* before *more*.
entries.pattern: Let's give it a couple more minutes (for people to join)
examples: Only four of us are here so far. **Let's give it a couple more minutes** before we start.
The tour guide checked her watch: "**Let's give it a couple more minutes** for the last group."
Dinner's ready, but Sam's train is late, so **let's give it a couple more minutes**.

drill.sentence: It's 9:01 and people are still joining the call, so {{let's give it a couple more minutes}} before we begin.
drill.hint: we'll wait a short while for others — informal, seven words (not *wait …* or *… a few …*)

mistake.wrong: Let's give it a couple of more minutes.
mistake.right: Let's give it a couple more minutes.
mistake.why: Before *more*, *a couple* takes no *of*: *a couple more minutes*, but *a couple of minutes*.

entries.related: *let's wait a few minutes* — plainer; *we'll start at five past* — gives a fixed time; *hang on* — informal, wait a moment.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To discuss all the planned topics of a meeting in the time available.
entries.usage: Common when the chair is worried about time: *We need to get through the agenda by noon* or *We didn't get through the whole agenda*. It stresses effort and reaching the end, as if the agenda were a task to finish. *Cover the agenda* is more neutral.
entries.pattern: get through the (whole) agenda (by + time / in + time)
examples: If we want to **get through the agenda** by noon, we'll need to keep each update short.
We never **got through the agenda**, so the PTA's vote on the field trip was pushed to May.
Even with three new members asking questions, the board **got through the agenda** in an hour.

drill.sentence: Please keep your comments short; there are eleven items, and we need to {{get through the agenda}} before four.
drill.hint: reach the end of every planned topic in time (not *cover*, *finish* or *go …*)

entries.related: *cover* — discuss, more neutral; *go through the agenda* — review it item by item; *run out of time* — not finish.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: A quick, informal vote or count in which people raise their hands to show their answer.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, classes, conferences and community meetings: *Let's take a show of hands*. It is quick and public, so it is not used for sensitive or secret decisions. Typical patterns are *by a show of hands* and *Can I get a show of hands?* to see, for example, how many people have done something.
entries.pattern: (take / ask for) a show of hands; by a show of hands
examples: Quick **show of hands**: who's already used the new booking system?
The club members voted by **a show of hands** to raise the yearly fee.
The teacher asked for **a show of hands** to see who had finished the reading.

drill.sentence: We don't need a secret ballot for something this small; let's just decide by {{a show of hands}}.
drill.hint: people raising their arms to vote (not *a vote*)

entries.related: *a secret ballot* — a private, written vote; *a straw poll* — an informal vote to see opinions; *a quick poll* — common in online meetings.
